meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: Before matching, GLP-1 RA users had markedly higher obesity prevalence (BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m2: 13.21% vs 3.04% in insulin and 4.87% in metformin) and higher socioeconomic/insurance status (undergraduate and above: 26.07% vs 15.65% in insulin and 11.94% in metformin; citizen health insurance: 75.60% vs 59.60% and 54.96%). Key clinical confounders including baseline diabetes duration, HbA1c (missing in 90.52% to 91.79%), and lifestyle factors were unadjusted or matched using 'unspecified' categories, pushing hazard ratios away from the null.

domains.direction_justification: Restricting analysis to strict monotherapy users (accumulative other diabetic prescriptions <6 months across multi-year follow-up) excluded 362,035 patients due to missing prescription data and selected an unrepresentative subset of patients with atypical prescribing patterns.

findings.mechanism: Conditioning cohort entry and maintenance on long-term monotherapy in a chronic disease where multidrug escalation is standard care introduces selection bias and potential conditioning on post-baseline treatment response.

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Acute side effects (diarrhea, emesis, dermatitis, dizziness, arrhythmia) leading to discontinuation were explicitly treated as competing risk events in Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models, distorting event probabilities and inflating sHRs for non-censored adverse outcomes.

findings.title: Inappropriate modeling of post-exposure side effects as competing risks
findings.mechanism: Treating treatment interruption/discontinuation due to mild acute symptoms as competing events rather than censoring or standard survival endpoints inappropriately alters the subdistribution hazard for outcomes like acute nephritis (sHR 3.20) and kidney failure (sHR 3.73).
evidence: Competing events systematically defined as a binomial variable activated by any incidence of acute symptoms including diarrhea/emesis, dermatitis tetter, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users have higher healthcare contact and diagnostic surveillance for known adverse effects (thyroid nodules, pancreatic enzymes, renal function tests), increasing detection of asymptomatic or incidental conditions (e.g. thyroid cancer sHR 2.25, thyroid dysfunction sHR 1.27, skin cysts sHR 1.50).

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias using unvalidated regex/ICD-10
findings.mechanism: Outcomes were identified via ICD-10 and unvalidated regular expressions across outpatient/inpatient records without blinded chart adjudication, making the study susceptible to ascertainment bias in intensively monitored patients on newer injectable drugs.

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Multiple statistical testing across more than 20 individual disease endpoints and drug-specific subgroups without multiplicity correction favors the selective highlighting of extreme effect estimates (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65-48.98).

findings.title: Multiplicity of tested adverse outcomes and subgroup analyses
findings.mechanism: Screening dozens of outcomes across six physiological systems without pre-specified protocol registration increases the probability of false-positive associations driven by sparse event counts.
evidence: Leukemia sHR 15.09 (95% CI 4.65-48.98) noted after 12 months, acknowledged by authors as potential 'random bias caused by a relatively low incidence rate and cases'

overall.summary: This retrospective observational study evaluated adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use compared to metformin and insulin monotherapy in Shenzhen, China. The study is at very high overall risk of bias due to profound missingness in core clinical confounders (HbA1c missing in >90% of participants, BMI and demographic variables missing in >30% and handled via missing-indicator matching), severe surveillance/detection bias for outcomes like thyroid cancer and renal failure in patients prescribed novel injectable therapies, artificial cohort restriction to continuous monotherapy users, and the unconventional treatment of post-exposure side effects as competing risks. These methodological limitations substantially inflate subdistribution hazard ratios away from the null.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event numbers and person-time per outcome across exposed and matched comparator arms (only subdistribution hazard ratios and demographic counts are reported).
Complete baseline glycemic control (HbA1c) and kidney function (eGFR/creatinine) data to control for baseline microvascular disease and indication severity.
Data on frequency of diagnostic testing (e.g., thyroid ultrasound, serum lipase/amylase, serum creatinine) across treatment groups to quantify surveillance bias.

baseline_comparability.summary: In the unmatched cohort, GLP-1 RA users were younger, had higher socioeconomic/insurance status, and were substantially more obese than insulin or metformin users. Propensity score matching balanced demographics and BMI categories, but key outcome predictors including baseline renal function, lipid profiles, and HbA1c (>90% missing) remained unmeasured or unadjusted, pushing adverse risk estimates away from the null.
